title: 2024 Smart-Meter Electricity Consumption Report
executive_summary: Analysis of 1,428 smart-meter readings across 2024 reveals total consumption of 1,207,700 kWh. Industrial sites dominate usage, Q4 was the highest-consumption quarter, and the second half of the year saw a modest 4.7% increase over the first. Tariff split is near-even, and a notable negative correlation exists between temperature and commercial energy use.

key_findings.statement: Across all 1,428 readings in 2024, total electricity consumption reached 1,207,700 kWh, with a mean of 845.7 kWh per reading.
Industrial buildings accounted for 995,362 kWh (82.4% of total), far exceeding Commercial at 196,367 kWh (16.3%) and Residential at 15,971 kWh (1.3%).
Q4 was the highest-consumption quarter at 352,882 kWh, followed by Q1 (319,678 kWh), Q2 (270,277 kWh), and Q3 (264,863 kWh), indicating a mid-year trough and year-end peak.
Second-half consumption (617,745 kWh) exceeded first-half consumption (589,955 kWh) by 4.7%, representing an increase of approximately 27,790 kWh.
On hot days (temperature ≥ 25°C), 19 commercial readings were recorded with a mean consumption of 415.3 kWh per reading.

The median reading was 406.8 kWh with a standard deviation of 913.4 kWh, indicating high variability. Mean recorded temperature was 11.6°C; 62 readings had missing temperature data. Commercial sites show a strong negative Pearson correlation of −0.64 between temperature and energy use, suggesting higher commercial consumption in cooler conditions.
Off-peak tariff accounted for 608,076 kWh versus 599,624 kWh at peak tariff (49.7% of total). Across 12 distinct meters, the highest single-meter consumption was 252,241 kWh.

limitations: The cleaning stage validation failed, meaning the cleaned dataset may contain residual data quality issues (e.g., duplicates, incorrect values, or improperly handled outliers) that could affect all downstream metrics.
62 readings have missing temperature_c values, which excludes them from temperature-related analyses and may introduce bias in correlation and mean temperature calculations.
Only 19 hot-day commercial readings (temperature ≥ 25°C) were available, making the hot-day commercial mean statistically fragile and not broadly generalisable.
With only 12 distinct meters, the dataset may not be representative of the broader meter population, and the highest single-meter figure (252,241 kWh) could reflect a single atypical site.
The negative commercial temperature–consumption correlation is observational; no causal inference can be drawn without controlling for confounding variables such as building size or occupancy.
conclusion: Industrial sites drive the vast majority of 2024 electricity consumption. Demand follows a U-shaped quarterly pattern with a mid-year trough and Q4 peak, and second-half usage grew 4.7% over the first half. The near-even peak/off-peak tariff split offers limited optimisation headroom. The strong negative temperature–commercial consumption correlation warrants further investigation into heating-driven demand. Data quality concerns from the failed cleaning stage should be resolved before acting on these findings.
